blocks.text: Imagine searching through a phone book with thousands of names. How can we ensure that the search is efficient, even as we add more names?

blocks.markdown: Balanced trees are a class of data structures that maintain their height as low as possible. This ensures that operations such as insertion, deletion, and lookup can be performed efficiently, typically in $O(\log n)$ time. In this lesson, we will explore why balance is crucial and how rotations help maintain it.

blocks.title: Balanced Tree
blocks.text: A balanced tree is a binary search tree (BST) where the height of the left and right subtrees of any node differ by at most one.

blocks.markdown: The key property of balanced trees is that they maintain a logarithmic height relative to the number of nodes, $n$. This is crucial because the height of the tree directly affects the time complexity of operations.

blocks.caption: The height $h$ of a balanced tree is logarithmic in the number of nodes $n$.

blocks.title: Why Balancing Ensures $O(\log n)$ Operations
blocks.prompt: Consider a balanced binary search tree with 15 nodes. What is the maximum height of this tree?

steps.text: A balanced tree has a height of $O(\log n)$. We start by calculating $\log_2(15)$.
Calculate $\log_2(15) \approx 3.91$. The maximum height is the ceiling of this value, which is 4.

blocks.answer: The maximum height of the tree is 4.

blocks.markdown: Rotations are operations used in balanced trees to maintain their height after insertions or deletions. A rotation changes the structure of the tree without affecting the in-order sequence of elements.

blocks.title: Rotation
blocks.text: A rotation is a tree operation that changes the structure of the tree to restore balance while preserving the binary search tree property.

blocks.title: Right Rotation
blocks.prompt: Perform a right rotation on the following subtree rooted at node $A$ with left child $B$.

steps.text: Identify the nodes involved: $A$ is the root, $B$ is the left child of $A$.
Make $B$ the new root of the subtree. $A$ becomes the right child of $B$.
The right child of $B$, if any, becomes the left child of $A$.

blocks.answer: After the right rotation, $B$ is the root, and $A$ is the right child of $B$.

blocks.markdown: Balanced binary search trees (BSTs) and hash tables are both used for data storage and retrieval, but they have different performance characteristics and use cases.

blocks.caption: Comparison of Balanced BST and Hash Table

blocks.title: When to Use Balanced Trees
blocks.text: Use balanced trees when ordered access is required and the dataset size can vary significantly.

points: Balanced trees maintain $O(\log n)$ operations by keeping the height low.
Rotations are used to restore balance after insertions or deletions.
Balanced BSTs provide ordered access, unlike hash tables.
